name: Nicholas II Alexandrovich
role: Emperor under whom Russia leased Kwantung, founded Dalny and lost the war with Japan
bio: Born on 6 (18) May 1868 at Tsarskoye Selo, he came to the throne in 1894. As heir, he made his Eastern journey in 1890–1891; at Ōtsu on 11 May 1891 New Style, the policeman Tsuda Sanzō wounded his head with a sabre. On the return journey he inaugurated the Ussuri Railway at Vladivostok, the beginning of the Trans-Siberian. He directed Far Eastern policy personally: the Chinese Eastern Railway, the Kwantung lease in 1898, the Russian name Dalny for the new port, and the occupation of Manchuria in 1900. In 1903 he effectively removed ministers from Far Eastern affairs, establishing Alekseyev’s viceroyalty, backing Bezobrazov’s group and retiring Witte to an honorary post. He did not want war and long doubted Japan would dare fight, but the failure to withdraw from Manchuria and prolonged negotiations made it almost inevitable. The Treaty of Portsmouth transferred Kwantung, with Port Arthur and Dalny, to Japan. Nicholas pardoned Stessel in May 1909. He was executed with his family in Yekaterinburg in July 1918.
quote: “God grant that the fears expressed here do not come true!” — annotation on N. I. Grodekov’s memorandum about another war with Japan

name: Sergei Yulyevich Witte
role: Finance minister, architect of the Chinese Eastern Railway project and founder of Dalny; signed the Treaty of Portsmouth
bio: Born in Tiflis in 1849, Witte graduated in physics and mathematics from Novorossiysk University and by 1886 managed the Southwestern Railways. In 1892 he became transport minister, then finance minister for eleven years: the state spirits monopoly, the gold ruble of 1897 and Trans-Siberian construction. In 1896 he negotiated with Li Hongzhang and secured the Chinese Eastern Railway concession. He opposed taking Port Arthur but arranged the lease once the decision was made. In Kwantung his main concern was Dalny, built with its port by the railway company using Finance Ministry money, while Port Arthur’s defences lacked funds. He toured Manchuria and visited Dalny in 1902. Removed as minister in August 1903, he negotiated at Portsmouth in 1905, avoiding an indemnity but conceding southern Sakhalin and the Kwantung lease to Japan. He gained a count’s title and the nickname “Count Half-Sakhalin”, and drafted the October Manifesto. He died on 28 February (13 March) 1915.
quote: “That madman Bezobrazov has vanished, gone under” — Witte to Kuropatkin, 1904

name: Yevgeny Ivanovich Alekseyev
role: First chief administrator of Kwantung; from 1903, Viceroy of the Far East, based in Port Arthur
bio: Born in 1843, officially the son of Lieutenant Commander Ivan Alekseyev, he was dogged by rumours that Alexander II was his father. After naval college he sailed around the world and served as naval attaché in Paris in the 1880s. He commanded the Pacific Fleet from 1895. In 1899 he became Kwantung’s first chief administrator, combining army, navy and civilian authority. The territory was divided into five districts, with Chinese officials retained as intermediaries. He directed Russian forces against the Boxers in 1900. As Far Eastern viceroy from August 1903, he oversaw negotiations with Japan, China and Korea. His instruction to avoid risks and preserve the squadron restricted the fleet at Port Arthur. He lost supreme command after the Shahe in October 1904; the viceroyalty was abolished in 1905. His rival Witte’s memoirs did much to shape his reputation. He died in Yalta on 27 May (9 June) 1917.
quote: “He had sound judgment and a strong will” — naval historian V. Gribovsky on Alekseyev

name: Li Hongzhang (李鸿章)
role: Qing statesman who developed the Beiyang Fleet base at Lüshunkou and signed the Chinese Eastern Railway and Kwantung lease agreements
bio: Born in Hefei, Anhui, in 1823. From 1870 he spent almost a quarter-century governing the capital province of Zhili and overseeing northern ports, building arsenals, telegraphs, steamship companies and the Beiyang Fleet. In the 1880s, the fishing village of Lüshunkou became its base, with docks and batteries: the future Port Arthur, captured by Japan in a single day in 1894. At Shimonoseki, while negotiating peace in 1895, Li was wounded by a Japanese extremist, and Japan reduced the indemnity from 300 to 200 million taels. At Nicholas II’s coronation in 1896 he signed an alliance against Japan and agreed to the Chinese Eastern Railway; he was promised 3 million rubles. In spring 1898 he signed the Kwantung lease convention and received 500,000 rubles. As governor in Canton in 1900 he refused Cixi’s order to wage war on the powers; in 1901 he signed the Boxer Protocol. He died in Beijing in November 1901 without signing the Manchurian agreement sought by St Petersburg.
quote: “Use barbarians to control barbarians” — a principle Li Hongzhang followed throughout his life

name: Alexander Mikhailovich Bezobrazov
role: State secretary, leader of the “Bezobrazov circle” and the Yalu timber venture
bio: Born in 1853, or 1855 according to other sources, he retired as a captain in the Cavalier Guards. Grand Duke Alexander Mikhailovich introduced him to Nicholas II in 1898. Bezobrazov proposed a “peaceful conquest” of Korea through private enterprise modelled on the British East India Company. Its foundation was a timber concession on the Yalu and Tumen rivers, obtained by Vladivostok merchant Julius Briner in 1896 and purchased in 1898 against Witte’s opposition. Soldiers disguised as loggers went to the Yalu and built fortifications. Grand dukes, the dowager empress and the treasury supplied funds: 2 million rubles went to the concession in the first half of 1903. Bezobrazov became state secretary on 6 May 1903. That August Witte lost the Finance Ministry and Viceroy Alekseyev was instructed to discuss economic matters with Bezobrazov. He left for Switzerland in early 1904 and held no further role after 1905. He died in exile in Paris in 1931. Historians dispute whether he was a principal cause of the war or a convenient scapegoat.
quote: “A great fantasist” with boundless self-confidence — V. I. Gurko on Bezobrazov

name: Vyacheslav Konstantinovich von Plehve
role: Interior minister in 1902–1904 and ally of Bezobrazov’s circle; the remark about a “small victorious war” is attributed to him
bio: Born in Meshchovsk, Kaluga province, in 1846, he graduated in law from Moscow University and worked in the prosecution service. After Alexander II’s assassination he headed the Police Department and crushed Narodnaya Volya, later serving as state secretary and pursuing Russification in Finland. He became interior minister in April 1902 after Sipyagin’s assassination. A rival of Witte, he supported Bezobrazov’s group; some historians regard him as its inspiration. The remark “we need a small victorious war” survives only at second hand, in a 1907 book under the pseudonym A. Morskoy and Witte’s memoirs, published in 1922. Witte had not heard it himself, quoting Kuropatkin; no independent confirmation exists. Plehve was killed by Socialist Revolutionary Yegor Sozonov’s bomb on Izmailovsky Avenue, St Petersburg, on 15 July 1904. Yevno Azef and Boris Savinkov directed the Combat Organisation’s operation. Two days later Japanese troops reached Port Arthur’s immediate approaches and the siege began.
quote: “To hold back the revolution, we need a small victorious war” — words attributed to Plehve in Witte’s memoirs; authenticity unproven

name: Alexei Nikolayevich Kuropatkin
role: War minister in 1898–1904, then commander of the Manchurian Army and commander-in-chief
bio: War minister from 1898 to 1904, Kuropatkin opposed Witte’s policy of withdrawal from Manchuria. According to Witte, he welcomed the Boxer Rebellion as a pretext for occupation. In 1903 General D. I. Subotich wrote to him that Vladivostok was enough for Russia and its Manchurian policy would bring ruin. Kuropatkin took command of the Manchurian Army at the outbreak of war and succeeded Alekseyev as commander-in-chief after the Shahe in October 1904. The army retreated through the Yalu, Liaoyang, Shahe, Sandepu and Mukden in February–March 1905, after which he was removed. The headquarters’ 1905 album shows him thanking Putilov Hill’s heroes and inspecting a hospital train. His papers are in the Russian State Military Historical Archive, Collection 165. He deposited his diary for 1904–1906 in the military archive in autumn 1915 before leaving for the front; Krasny Arkhiv published it in 1922–1935. In 1913 he proposed moving the border so that the Gobi Desert would separate Russia from China.
quote: “I am very glad. This will give us a pretext to seize Manchuria” — Kuropatkin on the Boxer Rebellion, as reported by Witte

name: Roman Isidorovich Kondratenko
role: Commander of Port Arthur’s land defences, the “soul of the defence”
bio: Born in Tiflis on 30 September (12 October) 1857, the tenth child of a retired major. He graduated from the Nikolayev Engineering School, Nikolayev Engineering Academy and General Staff Academy, finishing both academies in the first category. He commanded the 20th Rifle Regiment, with which he first saw Port Arthur in 1900. In November 1903 he took over the 7th East Siberian Rifle Brigade there; from the war’s start Stessel entrusted him with the entire land front. He completed defences under fire, installed guns from stores and ships, organised hand-grenade manufacture and supported inventors of mine throwers. On 18 September 1904 he warned Stessel not to expect timely relief; his letter went no further. He died with eight officers in Fort No. II’s officers’ casemate on 2 (15) December 1904, struck by an 11-inch shell. His remains were moved to the Alexander Nevsky Monastery in 1905. A Japanese memorial marks his death.
quote: “No assault can be terrifying if we resolve to fulfil the oath we have sworn to the very end” — Kondratenko’s order after the fighting at the Wolf Hills, July 1904

name: Anatoly Mikhailovich Stessel
role: Commander of the Kwantung Fortified Region; signed Port Arthur’s surrender
bio: During the war, Stessel commanded the Kwantung Fortified Region; K. N. Smirnov commanded the fortress, and R. I. Kondratenko led the land defences, entrusted with the whole land front from the first days. During the first assault Stessel wrote that Kondratenko should not accompany individual companies and asked him by telephone not to go into combat personally. He took no action on Kondratenko’s letter of 18 September 1904 proposing a truthful report to the tsar. On 20 December 1904 (2 January 1905), he signed the surrender against the military council’s decision to hold out. Around 23,000–25,000 men became prisoners. Sentenced to death for surrendering the fortress, he received a commuted sentence of ten years and was pardoned by Nicholas II in May 1909. The verdict contained no charge of selling the fortress, central to Stepanov’s Port Arthur. The defence’s most disputed figure, he inspired a 1905 joke: “Your turn to deal! — I’ve already surrendered.”
quote: “He must not be sent with individual companies. His loss would be irreplaceable” — Stessel on Kondratenko during the first assault

name: Stepan Osipovich Makarov
role: Fleet commander at Port Arthur in February–March 1904; died aboard Petropavlovsk
bio: Vice admiral, oceanographer and ship designer who initiated the icebreaker Yermak. He arrived at Port Arthur in late February 1904, replacing Vice Admiral O. V. Stark, under whom the squadron had been caught by the Japanese night attack. In 36 days of command he restored confidence and began taking the squadron to sea. On 10 March 1904 he appointed Rear Admiral K. P. Jessen to command the Vladivostok Cruiser Detachment. On 31 March (13 April), his flagship Petropavlovsk struck a mine and sank. Captain Lilje, who witnessed it, wrote that she disappeared “within some three minutes”. The admiral, around 650 crew and the painter Vasily Vereshchagin, aboard to make sketches, died; around 80 survived. Vitgeft succeeded him, and the squadron returned to the caution prescribed by the viceroy. In time-travel novels, Makarov usually survives.

name: Wilhelm Karlovich Vitgeft
role: The viceroy’s naval chief of staff; commanded the First Squadron after Makarov and died in the Yellow Sea battle
bio: Rear admiral and naval chief of staff to Viceroy Alekseyev. Leaving a meeting on the evening of 26 January 1904, hours before the Japanese attack, he said extensive precautions for the squadron were unnecessary. Negotiations were still under way and war without a declaration seemed unthinkable. After Makarov’s death in April 1904 he effectively took command. An experienced staff officer, he did not consider himself a fleet commander; the viceroy’s injunction to avoid risk and preserve the squadron reinforced his caution. On 28 July (10 August) 1904, directly ordered from St Petersburg, he attempted to break through to Vladivostok. A Japanese shell struck the bridge of his flagship Tsesarevich during the Yellow Sea battle and killed him. With damaged steering, Tsesarevich circled and broke the formation, leaving the squadron without effective command. Some ships were interned at Qingdao, Shanghai and Saigon; the main force returned to Port Arthur to be destroyed later by siege howitzers. None reached Vladivostok.
quote: “…since there will be no war” — Vitgeft on the evening of 26 January 1904, hours before the Japanese destroyer attack

name: Konstantin Ivanovich Velichko
role: Military engineer who designed Port Arthur’s land defences
bio: Military engineer, fortification specialist and professor at the Nikolayev Engineering Academy. In 1898–1900 he designed Port Arthur’s system of forts and intermediate works, approved on 18 January 1900. It included six forts, I–VI, as heavily armed strongpoints with garrisons of up to two companies, and five intermediate fortifications held mainly by infantry. Only about 4.25 million of the budgeted 15 million rubles was provided before the war. Velichko reduced concrete thickness: shelter vaults reached 0.9 metres, designed against 6-inch shells. Planning for a garrison no larger than 11,300, he placed the line a few kilometres from town, leaving several heights outside it, including 203 Metre Hill. The land-front forts were unfinished when war began; Fort VI remained on paper. The design was later criticised, but in 1900 neither a months-long siege nor 280 mm howitzers had been anticipated.

name: Vladimir Vasilyevich Sakharov
role: Engineer who built Dalny’s port and became its first city governor
bio: A harbour engineer who built Vladivostok’s commercial port before coming to Kwantung. From 1899 he designed and built the port in Victoria Bay, within Dalian Bay, then became Dalny’s city governor. The Chinese Eastern Railway Company built port and city; the first harbour phase cost 10.8 million rubles, and within three years Dalny ranked second in China for cargo turnover, after Shanghai. The city gained Manchuria’s first power station, water mains and a telephone network. At the outbreak of war, State Councillor Sakharov volunteered for Port Arthur. A caption to his 1904 magazine portrait says he served as a captain under General Fok and contributed much to the defence through his ingenuity. He died of typhus in the fortress in October 1904, aged 45. The Japanese captured his port almost intact in May 1904 and used it to supply the siege army, then developed Dairen along the Russian plan for forty years.

name: Kazimierz Geliodorovich Skolimowski
role: Architect of Dalny’s general plan
bio: Polish architect who designed Dalny’s general plan. Born in Brodnia near Łódź in 1862, he studied at St Petersburg’s Academy of Arts and in Berlin and Munich. In 1899, on Alexander Pomerantsev’s recommendation, he was invited to design Dalny. Rejecting a rectangular grid, he proposed a radial layout: circular Nikolayevskaya Square, 213 metres across, with ten avenues. He presented a new general plan in 1900 and detailed design in 1903, considering terrain, street views and living conditions. A park separated the European and Chinese towns. His report “On Designing the Plan of the City of Dalny” was delivered on 3 (16) February 1904 and published in Zodchiy, Nos. 12–14. Returning to Poland, he became Kalisz’s city architect. He died on 28 December 1923 while inspecting the icy roof of the town hall under construction. His radial layout still shapes central Dalian.
portrait_note: Portrait from the channel’s new post. Patronymic and life dates updated from the publication of 11 November 2026.

name: Mikhail Ivanovich Lilje
role: Military engineer who built Kwantung’s fortifications and wrote the Diary of the Siege of Port Arthur
bio: Born into a noble family in 1868, Lilje graduated from the Nikolayev Engineering Academy and was posted to Port Arthur in 1898. From 1900 he directed construction for the Kwantung Engineering Administration, building the works he would later defend. He kept a diary throughout the siege, from January 1904 to January 1905. On the first night he wrote that the squadron was “completely unprepared for battle”; on 31 March he witnessed Petropavlovsk’s sinking. In November he recorded scurvy and command disputes, calling 203 Metre Hill “Arthur’s Calvary”. On 20 December he explained the night’s explosions: “Our sailors were blowing up all our ships, cranes, and so on.” Decorated after the war with the Orders of St Anne and St Vladimir with swords, he became a lieutenant colonel and built defences in Finland during the First World War. He emigrated to France after 1917 and died in 1941. He sent his manuscript to the USSR, where it was held in the Lenin Library, nearly lost during preparations for a 1992 edition and finally published from a surviving copy in 2002.
quote: “All this muddle vividly illustrates our order and preparedness for war” — diary, 28 January 1904

name: Nogi Maresuke
role: Commander of the Japanese Third Army, which besieged Port Arthur
bio: Japanese general commanding the Third Army, which conducted Port Arthur’s land siege from summer 1904. Foreign war correspondents worked at his headquarters: on the first assault’s morning he received them and asked an interpreter to state each man’s nationality and credentials. The army made four general assaults; Russian estimates put Japan’s losses at Port Arthur above 110,000. Nogi lost both sons in the campaign. After the failed August assault, 280 mm howitzers were brought from Japanese coastal fortresses and began firing in late September 1904. On 22 November (5 December), the army took 203 Metre Hill, enabling siege artillery to destroy the squadron in the harbour’s inner basins. The fortress surrendered on 20 December 1904 (2 January 1905). Nogi and his wife died by suicide on the day of Emperor Meiji’s funeral in 1912.

name: Karl Petrovich Jessen
role: Commander of the Vladivostok Cruiser Detachment, whose raids interrupted the delivery of siege howitzers to Port Arthur
bio: Rear admiral appointed by Makarov on 10 March 1904 to command the Vladivostok Cruiser Detachment: Rossiya, Gromoboi, Rurik and Bogatyr. Its task was to attack Japanese trade and communications with Korea. On 2 (15) June, under temporary commander Vice Admiral P. A. Bezobrazov, the cruisers sank Hitachi Maru and Izumi Maru in the Korea Strait; Sado Maru ran aground. Hitachi Maru and Sado Maru carried 18 siege howitzers of 280 mm for Port Arthur. In July Jessen raided Japan’s eastern coast and sank the British steamer Knight Commander 15 miles from the entrance to Tokyo Bay; a London prize court upheld the capture. On 1 (14) August off Ulsan, the detachment, sailing to meet the squadron attempting to escape Port Arthur, encountered Kamimura’s cruisers and lost Rurik. Jessen received the Order of St George, 4th Class, and brought the surviving ships to the Baltic after the war. He was subsequently reprimanded, faced trial and retired in 1908.

name: Kamimura Hikonojō
role: Japanese vice admiral who commanded the cruisers opposing the Vladivostok detachment
bio: Japanese vice admiral commanding an armoured-cruiser squadron. His main task in 1904 was to counter the Vladivostok cruisers, which attacked Japanese transports in the Sea of Japan and off Japan’s Pacific coast. On 2 (15) June, Russian cruisers sank transports carrying 280 mm siege howitzers for the army at Port Arthur; the Japanese navy had to commit an entire squadron against Vladivostok. On 1 (14) August off Ulsan, Kamimura intercepted Jessen’s force as it sailed to meet the squadron breaking out of Port Arthur. Hits to Rurik’s stern disabled her steering; she fell behind and was scuttled. More than 200 died, while the Japanese rescued around 625 sailors. Rossiya and Gromoboi returned to Vladivostok badly damaged, effectively ending the cruiser campaign. Kamimura is a historical character in Valentin Pikul’s Cruisers.

name: Dean Ivanovich Subotich
role: An early administrator of Kwantung, later Governor-General of the Amur region; proposed returning Dalny and Port Arthur to China
bio: A general of Serbian origin. In the first year of the Russian lease he headed Kwantung after Admiral F. V. Dubasov, until authority passed to Y. I. Alekseyev in 1899. He later succeeded N. I. Grodekov as Governor-General of the Amur region. In 1903, months before the war, he sent War Minister Kuropatkin a memorandum historian M. V. Khodyakov considers the most clear-headed of the generals’ Manchurian plans. Subotich argued that Russia was a land power and Vladivostok was sufficient. A verst of the Chinese Eastern Railway cost 152,000 rubles, 80,000 more than in Transbaikalia; at least a billion had been invested in Manchuria. He proposed a deal modelled on the sale of Alaska: return southern Manchuria, including Dalny and Port Arthur, to China in exchange for northern Manchuria. Two years later Russia lost Dalny and Port Arthur to Japan under the Treaty of Portsmouth.
quote: Russia is heading “rather towards ruin and exhaustion” — Subotich’s memorandum to Kuropatkin, 1903

name: Alexander Nikolayevich Stepanov
role: Author of Port Arthur, awarded the Stalin Prize in 1946
bio: Born in Odessa in 1892 into a family of hereditary artillerymen. He graduated from the Sumy Cadet Corps and Mikhailovsky Artillery School, serving in the First World War with the Life Guards Rifle Artillery Battalion. He received six orders and, in February 1915, the St George Sword for fighting near Rudka-Skruda. He assembled Port Arthur from memoirs, veterans’ letters and his own front-line experience. The novel ran to 17 editions and over a million copies, receiving the Stalin Prize, First Class, in 1946. Stessel and Fok are traitors selling the fortress; Kondratenko is its last support. This scheme shaped popular views of the defence for decades. Stepanov claimed to have survived the siege as a boy at his father’s Electric Cliff battery, but in 2010 D. K. Nikolayev and O. V. Chistyakov demonstrated from archives that neither had been in the fortress. He died in 1965 and was buried at Novodevichy Cemetery.

name: Valentin Savvich Pikul
role: Author of Cruisers, a novel about the Vladivostok Cruiser Detachment
bio: Born in Leningrad on 13 July 1928, Pikul survived the siege’s first winter, graduated from the Solovki naval boys’ school in 1943 and served on the Northern Fleet destroyer Grozny until the war ended. Apart from a year at a naval preparatory school, he received no further education. He lived in Riga from 1962. His historical novels appeared in more than 500 editions, totalling around half a billion copies. Cruisers, written in 38 days for the Tsushima anniversary in 1985, received the Gorky State Prize of the RSFSR in 1988. It drew on V. Ye. Yegoryev’s 1939 study of Vladivostok cruiser operations. Historical figures Trusov, Dabich, Stemman, Jessen, P. A. Bezobrazov, Reitzenstein and Kamimura appear beside the invented midshipman Panafidin, who sinks with the real Rurik. Historians criticise this blending of fiction and documentary material. Pikul died in Riga on 16 July 1990.

name: Vikenty Vikentyevich Veresayev (Smidovich)
role: Military doctor in Manchuria and author of In the Russo-Japanese War
bio: Born in Tula in 1867, he graduated in history and philology from St Petersburg University and in medicine from Dorpat. His 1901 Notes of a Doctor caused a scandal through its frank account of medical errors and experiments on patients. Called from the reserve in 1904, he went to Manchuria as an army doctor and followed a field hospital through the whole war, including Mukden and the retreat, returning through revolutionary Siberia. In the Russo-Japanese War describes hospitals without patients, wounded men transported aimlessly for weeks, bureaucracy, the Mukden retreat and rallies at Trans-Siberian stations. Contemporaries accused him of being unpatriotic. Chapters appeared soon after the war; the full book in 1928. During the First World War he headed a military medical unit. Later he compiled Pushkin in Life and Gogol in Life and translated the Iliad and Odyssey. He received the Stalin Prize in 1943 and died in Moscow in June 1945.

name: Yevgeny Sergeyevich Botkin
role: Red Cross doctor with the Manchurian Army and author of Light and Shadows of the Russo-Japanese War
bio: Son of the physician S. P. Botkin, a doctor of medicine and lecturer at the Military Medical Academy. At the war’s outbreak he volunteered for Manchuria and headed the Red Cross medical service with the army in the field. Under shrapnel at Wafangou, now Wafangdian within Dalian, he carried wounded men and gave them his horse. For courage under fire he received military orders, including St Vladimir, 3rd and 2nd Class with swords. His letters to his wife appeared in Vestnik Evropy in 1908 and then as a book. Alongside dressing stations, typhus and dysentery that killed doctors and nurses, they contain observations of Manchurian life: counting and etiquette, houses, theatre and Mukden’s imperial tombs. In 1908 he became Nicholas II’s physician, followed the family into exile and was executed with them at the Ipatiev House in July 1918. The Russian Orthodox Church canonised him in 2016.
quote: “Now we feel war around us as one feels death in the house of a hopelessly ill patient” — letters to his wife

name: Leo Nikolayevich Tolstoy
role: Author of the anti-war essay Bethink Yourselves! (1904)
bio: In early 1904, as prayers and patriotic demonstrations greeted the war, the 75-year-old Tolstoy, who had defended Sevastopol’s Fourth Bastion in his youth, began Bethink Yourselves! It was ready by May. He wrote of peasants sent ten thousand versts to die for foreign land, priests blessing weapons, those stirring enthusiasm while remaining safe, and the soldier explaining his choice with “what else can you do?” The tsar appears more as an unhappy young man trapped in his own power. Tolstoy’s answer was for each person to heed their conscience and refuse to take part in killing. Russian newspapers rejected the essay. V. G. Chertkov sent it to England and The Times published it on 27 June (9 July) 1904. Moskovskiye Vedomosti replied with “The Maniac of Yasnaya Polyana”; Japan’s Heimin Shimbun translated it in August. The writer’s son Andrei volunteered for the war.
quote: “War again. Again sufferings needless and unprovoked, again lies, again universal stupefaction and the brutalisation of men” — opening of Bethink Yourselves!

name: Konstantin Dmitriyevich Balmont
role: Poet whose Our Tsar (1906) reduces the reign to Mukden and Tsushima
bio: Born in Vladimir province on 15 June 1867, Balmont was expelled from Shuya Gymnasium and Moscow University for involvement in political circles. In Boundlessness (1895), Burning Buildings (1900) and Let Us Be Like the Sun (1903) made him a leading Russian Symbolist. His poem “The Little Sultan” brought a two-year ban from capitals and university towns in 1901. The Japanese war and the 1905 revolution completed his politicisation. He left illegally for Paris in late 1905 and wrote “Our Tsar” in 1906. The reign is reduced to Mukden and Tsushima, beginning at Khodynka and destined to end on the scaffold. The poem appeared in Songs of an Avenger, Paris, 1907, but not in Russia. Balmont returned on 5 May 1913 under the Romanov tercentenary amnesty, visited Japan in 1916 and translated much tanka and haiku. Rejecting the October Revolution, he left for France in 1920 and died at Noisy-le-Grand near Paris on 23 December 1942.
quote: “Our tsar is Mukden, our tsar is Tsushima, / Our tsar is a bloody stain” — Our Tsar, 1906

name: Mikhail Osipovich Menshikov
role: Novoye Vremya journalist who wrote of the war as a test of the whole country
bio: A graduate of Kronstadt’s naval technical school, Menshikov served as navigator and hydrographer, compiling sailing directions before turning to journalism. When Nedelya closed, A. S. Suvorin recruited him to Novoye Vremya. His Letters to My Neighbours appeared two or three times weekly until spring 1917; subscribers received monthly booklets to bind into annual volumes. The 1902–1904 collection spans the Russo-Japanese War. In “Internal Defence” (1904), he wrote about the country’s condition rather than manoeuvres near Liaoyang: peacetime patriotism had fallen dangerously low, though it had not died. National existence, he argued, “must be defended beyond the fields of Manchuria”; defeats began at home, in offices, schools and taverns. He regarded the war as an examination the country had failed. Arrested at Valdai on 19 September 1918, he was shot without trial the next day.
quote: “The thunder of war was needed to wake our consciousness” — Internal Defence, 1904

name: Ilya Alexeyevich Shatrov
role: Bandmaster of the Mokshan Regiment and composer of On the Hills of Manchuria
bio: Son of a retired non-commissioned officer from Zemlyansk, Voronezh province; sources give his birth year as either 1879 or 1885. Bandmaster of the 214th Mokshan Infantry Regiment. In February 1905 near Mukden, with the regiment surrounded and ammunition running low, Colonel Pobyvanets ordered the colours and band forward. Shatrov led the musicians onto the parapet; they played a march under fire as the regiment broke through with bayonets. Seven hundred of four thousand men escaped; seven of 61 musicians survived, and Pobyvanets died. A year later at Zlatoust, Shatrov wrote The Mokshan Regiment on the Hills of Manchuria in their memory. Its first performance in Samara in spring 1908 met a cool response, but the score was reprinted 82 times in three years. Skitalets, S. Petrov, wrote the first lyrics. Shatrov later served with Red Army bands, returned to uniform in March 1945 and spent his final years conducting at Tambov’s Suvorov Military School. Promoted to Guards major on 20 April 1952, he died on 2 May that year.
quote: “Colours and band to the front!” — Colonel Pobyvanets’s order near Mukden, February 1905

name: Sergei Mikhailovich Prokudin-Gorsky
role: Photographer and printer who compiled and printed The Russo-Japanese War, 1904–1905 album
bio: A pioneer of Russian colour photography, producing more than 2,600 images in 1905–1915. The US Library of Congress acquired most from his sons in 1948. His connection with the Russo-Japanese War is often misunderstood: he is widely believed to have photographed Manchuria himself in 1904. In fact, on a General Staff commission, he prepared for printing The Russo-Japanese War, 1904–1905, published by the commander-in-chief’s headquarters in 1905: around 300 plates photographed by others. It shows the war from Manchurian army headquarters: Shahe fighting, Putilov Hill, XVII Corps positions, Rennenkampf’s detachment and the retreat from Mukden to Tieling. His workshops also printed the Album of the Wartime Life of the XVII Army Corps, 54 plates and 231 photographic reproductions, compiled by the Corps of Military Topographers. His contribution to both was printing; others took the pictures.

name: William Arthur
role: British naval officer after whom Lüshunkou harbour was named Port Arthur
bio: A Royal Navy lieutenant who took command of the gunboat HMS Algerine in June 1858 during the Second Opium War. The damaged vessel was towed into a small, unfortified fishing harbour where Arthur found shelter and charted the area. He did not name it himself: in August 1860 John Ward, commanding HMS Actaeon, named it after the lieutenant whose Algerine had been the first British ship to enter. The name took hold among the British and was adopted by Russia and other Western powers. After the lease of 1898 the fortress remained Port Arthur, although Nicholas II gave the neighbouring port the Russian name Dalny. The Chinese name Lüshunkou, “bay of smooth sailing”, traditionally dates to 1371. Arthur died in 1886, eighteen years before the siege. The claim that the port honoured Queen Victoria’s son Prince Arthur is not supported by documents.

name: Mikhail Yevgenyevich Mühlberg
role: “Port Arthur’s smallest child”, born in the besieged fortress
bio: Born in besieged Port Arthur on 13 November 1904, baptised the day after the surrender, Mikhail lived 52 days. He was buried in the Russian cemetery at Goshinji Temple, Nagasaki, where an unassuming grey stone still bears his inscription. His father, Second Lieutenant Yevgeny Mühlberg, was wounded in the defence and received the Order of St George. His grandmother worked in a hospital throughout the siege and became his godmother. Historian Dmitry Nikolayev reconstructed the family’s life through parish registers and archives in “Misha from Nagasaki”, Rodina, 2016, following its later history too. Officers’ families lived beside the garrison inside the fortress: women worked in hospitals and children were born under fire.

name: Vasily Vasilyevich Vereshchagin
role: Battle painter who died aboard Petropavlovsk with Admiral Makarov
bio: Born in Cherepovets, Vereshchagin graduated from the Naval Cadet Corps but chose the Academy of Arts over naval service. His paintings showed war through death and human suffering; he painted The Apotheosis of War in 1871. In 1874 he declined a professorship at the Academy. Working in Japan in autumn 1903, he painted Nikkō’s temples and warned of Russia’s unreadiness for war. He arrived at Port Arthur in spring 1904 and died on 31 March (13 April) when Petropavlovsk struck a mine. His body was not found.

name: Alexander Viktorovich Fok
role: Commander of the 4th East Siberian Rifle Division; succeeded Kondratenko as head of the fortress’s land defences
bio: A graduate of the Novgorod Arakcheyev Cadet Corps and Konstantinovsky Military School. He received the Order of St George, 4th Class, for crossing the Danube at Sistova in 1877 and served in the Chinese campaign of 1900–1901. In the Russo-Japanese War he commanded the 4th East Siberian Rifle Division; his actions at Jinzhou and unused reserves became disputed. During the siege he circulated staff “notes” offering advice and sharply criticising colleagues. After Kondratenko’s death, Stessel appointed him commander of the land defences. At the 1908 trial he was acquitted of the principal charges; a reprimand over the notes was dropped under the statute of limitations. He wounded Commandant Smirnov in a duel. He served with the Bulgarian army in 1912–1913 and lived in Bulgaria after the revolution. He died in 1926 and was buried near Svishtov.

name: Nikolai Matveyevich Yakovlev
role: Captain of Petropavlovsk who survived the loss of his ship
bio:
The flagship Petropavlovsk at Port Arthur had two different commanding officers: the admiral directed the squadron, while Captain Nikolai Yakovlev commanded the ship itself. When she sank on 31 March (13 April) 1904, Makarov died, but Yakovlev was rescued from the water. His war ended before the fortress fell: he was sent back to European Russia for treatment.

Born in 1856, he had served in the Black Sea and Baltic fleets, specializing in navigation and hydrography. Aboard Pamyat Azova he took part in the Far Eastern journey of the heir, Nicholas Alexandrovich.

After Port Arthur his career continued: command of the battleship Imperator Pavel I under construction, leadership of the Main Naval Staff and membership of the Admiralty Council. He became a full admiral in 1915 and in 1916 chaired the commission investigating the loss of Imperatritsa Mariya. Discharged in 1917, he died at Oryol in 1919, executed among a group of hostages.

name: Mikhail Pavlovich Molas
role: Makarov’s chief of staff, killed aboard Petropavlovsk
bio:
Admiral Stepan Makarov was not the only senior officer killed when Petropavlovsk sank on 31 March (13 April) 1904. His chief of staff, Rear Admiral Mikhail Molas, died with him. The staff prepared orders and supported the direction of the squadron; its loss was a separate, severe blow.

Born in 1852 into a naval family, Molas had commanded the gunboat Bobr and served on the Pacific Squadron’s staff. Promoted to rear admiral early in 1904, he reached Port Arthur as a junior flag officer and became Makarov’s chief of staff after the latter arrived. They had only a few weeks to work together. The sortie to assist Russian torpedo craft ended with the flagship returning towards Port Arthur and striking a Japanese minefield.

Molas’s story continued after his death. In 1913 remains identified as his during work on the wreck were ceremonially buried in Port Arthur’s Russian cemetery. The Navy Ministry’s representative was Nikolai Yakovlev, the captain who had survived the same disaster.

name: Eduard Nikolayevich Shchensnovich
role: Captain of Retvizan and organizer of Russian submarine training
bio:
At Port Arthur Eduard Shchensnovich commanded one of Russia’s strongest battleships; after the war he turned to vessels that could disappear beneath the surface. Between Retvizan and the Submarine Training Detachment lay a war that had exposed the changing dangers at sea.

Born in 1852, he graduated from the Naval School and the Mine Officers’ Class. Sent to the United States to supervise Retvizan’s construction, he later brought her to the Far East. A torpedo hit on the first night of the war put the battleship out of action, but repairs returned her to the squadron. In the battle of 28 July (10 August) 1904, after Vitgeft’s death disrupted the Russian formation, Shchensnovich headed Retvizan towards the Japanese ships. He was wounded; the approach was not completed, and the battleship returned to Port Arthur.

After captivity he headed the Submarine Training Detachment established at Libau in 1906. This new service required crews to learn the boats’ machinery, practise diving and build a shore organization. He died in 1910, having helped establish training for the first generations of Russian submariners.

name: Kazimir Filippovich Ketlinsky
role: Retvizan’s gunnery officer, later captain of Askold and naval commander on the Murman coast
bio:
Retvizan and Askold belonged to two different wars in Kazimir Ketlinsky’s life. In 1904 he was the battleship’s senior gunnery officer at Port Arthur; during the First World War he took command of the cruiser while she was being repaired in France and brought her to northern Russia.

Born at Mogilev-Podolsky in 1875, he graduated from the Naval Corps and trained in gunnery. Aboard Retvizan he was responsible for the gun service and helped defend both ship and fortress; in 1904 he became the squadron staff’s gunnery officer. After the war he continued artillery work and served in the Black Sea.

His command of Askold in 1916–1917 came at a difficult time: repairs dragged on, and after unrest aboard, four sailors were executed following a naval court sentence. In 1917 he became a rear admiral and headed the Murman Fortified Region and its naval detachment. He continued in office after the October Revolution, surviving arrest and release. In January 1918 unknown assailants mortally wounded him in Murmansk. A later account alone cannot establish who ordered the attack: the admiral’s name is much better known than the proven circumstances of his death.

name: Alexander Vladimirovich Razvozov
role: Retvizan’s torpedo officer and commander of the Baltic Fleet in 1917–1918
bio:
At Port Arthur Alexander Razvozov served as Retvizan’s torpedo officer, responsible for torpedo armament and associated shipboard equipment. Thirteen years later he would command the Baltic Fleet during the revolution.

Born at Reval in 1879 into a naval family, he graduated from the Naval Corps. Aboard Retvizan he helped repel Japanese attempts to block the harbour entrance with blockships and fought on 28 July (10 August) 1904. After the Russo-Japanese War he commanded destroyers and their formations in the Baltic, gaining experience of directing light forces during the First World War.

In 1917 he became a rear admiral and commander of the Baltic Fleet. The change of government did not immediately end his service: he remained after the October Revolution, but was removed in March 1918 following conflict with the Soviet naval leadership. Arrested in 1919, he died in prison at Petrograd in June 1920.

name: Robert Nikolayevich Viren
role: Captain of Bayan, later commander of the ships remaining at Port Arthur
bio:
At the start of the war in 1904 Robert Viren commanded Bayan, one of the most active cruisers of the Port Arthur Squadron. By the end of the siege he was directing the remaining naval forces in a harbour already under Japanese land artillery fire.

Born in 1856, he graduated from the Naval School, the Mine Officers’ Class and the Naval Academy. He took over Bayan while she was being built in France, brought her to the Far East and fought in 1904. The cruiser struck a mine that summer; her repairs coincided with the squadron’s dispersal after the Battle of the Yellow Sea. In August Viren became a rear admiral and was appointed to command the ships left at Port Arthur. As the fortress surrendered, surviving vessels were destroyed to prevent their capture intact.

After Japanese captivity Viren served in the Black Sea and Baltic. From 1909 he was chief commander of Kronstadt Port and military governor of Kronstadt, becoming an admiral in 1915. Sailors killed him during the February Revolution in March 1917. The captain of Bayan ended his career in another naval town, with no enemy fleet outside its harbour.

name: Ivan Konstantinovich Grigorovich
role: Captain of Tsesarevich, head of Port Arthur Port and the empire’s last Navy Minister
bio:
Ivan Grigorovich arrived at Port Arthur as captain of the new Tsesarevich and ended the siege as head of the port. That meant a different task: organizing repairs, supplies and the naval base’s work as fewer ships remained fit to fight.

Born at St Petersburg in 1853, he graduated from the Naval School, served in the Baltic and Pacific and was Russia’s naval agent in Britain. He supervised Tsesarevich’s construction in France before bringing her to the Far East. Torpedoed on the first night of the war, she stayed afloat. In spring 1904 Grigorovich took charge of the port and remained until the fortress surrendered. His supervision of French orders also connected him with Bayan’s construction, but did not make him a member of that cruiser’s crew.

After the war he headed ports and held senior naval posts. As Navy Minister in 1911–1917, he oversaw programmes to rebuild the fleet after defeat by Japan. After the revolution he lived in Russia, then France, where he died in 1930. His last office often overshadows his first Port Arthur task: before rebuilding the fleet as minister, he organized its repair and supply in a besieged port.

name: Nikolai Ottovich Essen
role: Captain of Novik and Sevastopol, later commander of the Baltic Fleet
bio:
At Port Arthur Nikolai Essen commanded two very different ships: the fast cruiser Novik and the slow battleship Sevastopol. The first called for speed and initiative in scouting; the second demanded persistence in defending a heavy ship in a blockaded base.

Born at St Petersburg in 1860, he graduated from the Naval School and had served for many years before the war. He took command of Novik in 1902 and brought her to the Far East. In January–February 1904 the cruiser fought in the opening actions off Port Arthur. In March Makarov transferred Essen to Sevastopol; Maximilian Schultz took over Novik. During the siege’s final weeks Sevastopol lay in White Wolf Bay, repelling Japanese torpedo-boat attacks. After suffering damage she was scuttled in deep water, preventing the Japanese from raising her with the other heavy ships in the harbour.

After the war Essen headed the Baltic naval forces and prepared them for another conflict. In 1914 he directed defensive minelaying in the Baltic. He died at Reval in May 1915, still in command of the fleet.

name: Maximilian Fyodorovich Schultz
role: Captain of Novik during the escape from Port Arthur and final action off Sakhalin
bio:
Novik’s last voyage from Port Arthur towards Sakhalin is associated with Maximilian Schultz. He replaced Nikolai Essen in March 1904 and that summer tried to reach Vladivostok after most of the Russian squadron returned to the besieged base.

Born at Kronstadt in 1862 into a naval family, he graduated from the Naval School and served aboard various Pacific ships. Sources also call him Mikhail: this is the same officer, not another captain of Novik. After the battle of 28 July (10 August) 1904, the cruiser left Port Arthur, briefly called at Tsingtao and continued around Japan. Coal supplies and machinery condition shaped her route as much as the enemy. Near Korsakov Post on Sakhalin, Novik fought the Japanese cruiser Tsushima and suffered damage. She was scuttled, leaving her men to reach friendly units without their ship.

Schultz continued serving, becoming a vice admiral and commander of the Siberian Flotilla. He retired after the revolution and was executed in 1919. References differ over the precise date and circumstances of that final episode; they cannot safely be turned into a single, certain scene.

name: Vsevolod Fyodorovich Rudnev
role: Captain of Varyag at the Battle of Chemulpo
bio:
On 9 February 1904 New Style, Vsevolod Rudnev brought Varyag out of the Korean port of Chemulpo to face a superior Japanese force. The gunboat Koreets accompanied her. The attempted breakout failed; the damaged cruiser returned to the anchorage and was scuttled after her crew transferred to foreign ships.

Born at Dünamünde in 1855 into a naval family, Rudnev graduated from the Naval School and served for many years aboard various vessels. Before Varyag he was senior assistant to the commander of Port Arthur Port, giving him a direct connection with the base. Chemulpo brought him the Order of St George and widespread fame. His reports of enemy losses nevertheless require separate checking: the story’s popularity cannot validate every early estimate.

In 1905 he retired as a rear admiral. He spent his final years in Tula province, died in 1913 and was buried at Savino. He is remembered chiefly as the captain of one battle, although decades of naval service lay behind that day.

name: Nikolai Karlovich Reitsenstein
role: Cruiser detachment commander who flew his flag aboard Askold
bio:
On the evening of 28 July (10 August) 1904, Askold, flying Nikolai Reitsenstein’s flag, broke through the Japanese forces and left the Port Arthur area. She never reached Vladivostok: damage forced her to seek refuge at Shanghai, where she was disarmed for the rest of the war.

Born in 1854, Reitsenstein graduated from the Naval School, specialized in torpedo and mine warfare, and served in the Pacific and Baltic. Around the turn of the century he supervised Askold’s construction in Germany and became her first captain. In spring 1904 he took command of the Port Arthur Squadron’s cruiser detachment. Two offices must be distinguished: Captain Konstantin Grammatchikov commanded Askold herself in battle, while Reitsenstein directed the formation. His breakout after the Russian line fell into disorder saved the cruiser, but did not accomplish the squadron’s original objective of reaching Vladivostok together.

After the war he held command and administrative posts in the Baltic, sat on the Admiralty Council and worked on coastal defence. Promoted to admiral in 1913, he died at Petrograd in 1916.

name: Vladimir Ivanovich Semyonov
role: Diana’s executive officer, Tsushima survivor and author of The Reckoning
bio:
Vladimir Semyonov saw the Russo-Japanese War from two squadrons. In 1904 he was executive officer of Diana at Port Arthur; in May 1905 he served with Rozhestvensky’s staff aboard Knyaz Suvorov at Tsushima. These experiences later became the basis of his books.

Born at St Petersburg in 1867, he graduated from the Naval School in 1887. Early in the war he briefly commanded the torpedo boat Reshitelny before joining Diana. After the Battle of the Yellow Sea the cruiser sailed to Saigon and was interned: disarmed in a neutral port for the rest of the war. Semyonov left the ship and joined the Second Pacific Squadron. Wounded at Tsushima, he was rescued from the flagship and taken prisoner.

The Reckoning, The Battle of Tsushima and The Price of Blood combined diary entries with later reflection on defeat. They are detailed eyewitness accounts, but express their author’s position: he defended Rozhestvensky, and his judgments cannot automatically be accepted as final verdicts on everyone else. He died in 1910. For readers of Diana’s story he remains the man who continued telling the war’s history after the cruiser herself ceased to take part in it.

name: Vasily Maximovich Zatsarenny
role: Commander of Pobeda during the defence of Port Arthur
bio:
Vasily Zatsarenny brought the battleship Pobeda to the Far East and was commanding her when war with Japan began. He had previously served in the Baltic, Black and Caspian Seas, graduated from the Mine Officer Class and commanded coast-defence ships. In 1901 he was given the new squadron battleship; in 1902–1903 Pobeda sailed from Kronstadt to Port Arthur.

Illness briefly forced Zatsarenny to hand command to Vladimir Sarnavsky in the summer of 1904. In the battle of 28 July, Old Style, he was again commanding Pobeda himself. After returning to the besieged port, the ship continued supporting the land defences until Japanese heavy artillery put her out of action. Her commander survived the fall of the fortress and captivity. He later headed the Nikolayev naval port, joined the Admiralty Council and became an admiral in 1913.

name: Nikolai Mikhailovich Ivanov
role: Commander of Tsesarevich at the Battle of the Yellow Sea
bio:
Nikolai Ivanov commanded Tsesarevich in the summer of 1904, when the battleship became the flagship of the Port Arthur Squadron. Squadron commander Wilgelm Vitgeft, his staff and the ship’s captain were aboard the same vessel. Their responsibilities differed: Vitgeft directed the entire squadron, while Ivanov was responsible for the battleship itself.

During the battle of 28 July, Old Style, a shell killed Vitgeft. Another hit near the conning tower soon wounded Ivanov and disrupted the ship’s control. Tsesarevich fell out of formation, and the squadron’s attempt to reach Vladivostok failed. Under the officers who succeeded the wounded Ivanov, the damaged ship sailed to German-held Qingdao. There the battleship was disarmed and remained in a neutral port until the war ended. V. Yu. Gribovsky’s study examines the battle damage and the captain’s decisions in detail.

name: Vladimir Fyodorovich Sarychev
role: Commander of Boyarin and later of Port Arthur’s coastal batteries
bio:
Vladimir Sarychev entered the war with experience that hardly foretold the notoriety to come. He had sailed on Skobelev, surveyed waters near New Guinea and commanded the gunboat Gilyak during the capture of the Taku forts in 1900. He then took command of the cruiser Boyarin, under construction in Denmark, and brought her to Port Arthur.

In the first days of the war, Boyarin struck a Russian mine near Dalny. Sarychev ordered the ship abandoned while she was still afloat. The unsuccessful effort to save her led to an investigation and trial: the captain was blamed for leaving too hastily. He nevertheless continued serving in the fortress’s defence. For the rest of the siege he commanded naval coastal batteries at the harbour entrance, before becoming a Japanese prisoner. He later served in the Baltic and died in Tallinn in 1924.

name: Vladimir Simonovich Sarnavsky
role: Commander of Pallada during the war of 1904
bio:
Vladimir Sarnavsky commanded Pallada during the defence of Port Arthur. Before the Russo-Japanese War, he had served on the Danube in 1877–1878, commanded torpedo boats and gunboats, trained in gunnery and studied at the Naval Academy. He took over Pallada shortly before hostilities began.

On the first night of the war, a torpedo put the cruiser out of action for a prolonged period. After repairs she returned to patrol duties and squadron sorties. In June Sarnavsky briefly replaced the ailing Zatsarenny aboard Pobeda, then resumed command of the cruiser. Pallada survived the July battle, returned to Port Arthur and was sunk in the harbour by siege artillery. After captivity, Sarnavsky continued serving in the Black Sea, headed its naval forces and the port of Sevastopol, and became an admiral in 1915.

name: K. A. Grammatchikov
role: Commander of Askold during the fighting and breakout of 1904
bio:
Captain First Rank Grammatchikov commanded Askold during the Russo-Japanese War. Cruiser-detachment commander Nikolai Reitsenstein was also aboard. These were distinct posts: the admiral directed the detachment, while the captain commanded the cruiser itself. Grammatchikov’s own reports preserve details of patrols on the outer roadstead and encounters with Japanese torpedo boats.

Following the Battle of the Yellow Sea on 28 July, Old Style, Askold broke out to the south, but damage prevented her from continuing to Vladivostok. The cruiser reached Shanghai and was interned: disarmed in a neutral port until the war ended. Grammatchikov later reached flag rank. His place in Port Arthur’s history is chiefly associated with a ship that escaped the blockade but could no longer return to the fighting.

name: Pavel Petrovich Ukhtomsky
role: Junior flag officer of the Port Arthur Squadron
bio:
Rear Admiral Pavel Ukhtomsky flew his flag in Peresvet as the Pacific Squadron’s junior flag officer. Before Port Arthur he had commanded ships, served as naval attaché in Britain and headed the staff of the Kronstadt naval port. He was appointed to the Far East in 1903.

In 1904 he twice had to assume the duties of a commander who had been killed. After the Petropavlovsk disaster he briefly succeeded Makarov; after Vitgeft’s death in the battle of 28 July, Old Style, he became the senior surviving flag officer. The damaged Peresvet returned to Port Arthur with most of the battleships. Ukhtomsky then led the squadron until handing command to Robert Viren. His wartime biography is thus associated with attempts to keep a formation under command after losing its leaders, rather than with a single victorious episode. He retired as a vice admiral in 1906.

name: Pyotr Nikolayevich Gubonin
role: Varyag midshipman wounded in the Battle of Chemulpo
bio:
Pyotr Gubonin joined Varyag as a very young officer. He came from a family known for building railways and developing the resort of Gurzuf: industrialist Pyotr Ionovich Gubonin was his grandfather. Naval service was chosen for the grandson. In 1897 his father applied for his admission to the Naval Corps; records of his studies and first appointments survive in the naval archive.

In the Battle of Chemulpo on 27 January (9 February) 1904, the midshipman suffered a serious leg wound. He was evacuated from Korea separately from the main crew, and returning to Russia took several months. A museum study reconstructs his journey from his service file and newspaper reports. Behind the familiar name Varyag is a junior officer whose short battle continued as a long recovery. His first name was Pyotr; the name “Pavel Nikolayevich” found in some retellings is mistaken.

name: Alexander Alexandrovich Lieven
role: Commander of Diana, who brought the cruiser to Saigon
bio:
Prince Alexander Lieven began in the Guards infantry before transferring to the navy, passing an officer examination and receiving a naval education. By the war with Japan he had commanded torpedo boats and gunboats. In 1904 he was given the cruiser Diana at Port Arthur.

After the battle of 28 July, Old Style, Diana became separated from the battleships returning to the fortress. Lieven took her south towards the French possessions in Indochina. The cruiser reached Saigon, where she was interned until the war ended. The captain described the battle and voyage in his own report, allowing readers to follow the route, decisions and condition of the ship. After the war Lieven helped examine its lessons and later headed the Naval General Staff. His career connected command of a ship in an unsuccessful campaign with efforts to establish what that campaign should teach the navy.

name: Vladimir Alexandrovich Lyubinsky
role: Senior gunnery officer of Pobeda
bio:
Lieutenant Vladimir Lyubinsky served as senior gunnery officer of the battleship Pobeda. He was responsible for the ship’s artillery: training crews, maintaining guns and organising fire. Pobeda’s officer list distinguishes him from her captain, Vasily Zatsarenny, and her junior gunnery officer, Pavel Vilken.

In 1904 the battleship took part in the Port Arthur Squadron’s fighting and the Battle of the Yellow Sea. Her gunners had to account for damaged weapons and ammunition expenditure, then prepare for new tasks on returning to the besieged base. Pobeda’s main armament consisted of 254 mm guns in two turrets; her secondary artillery was mounted separately. Behind the calibres listed in the ship’s records lay the work of officers and gun crews. Lyubinsky’s full name appears in the monograph on the Peresvet class and in the naval officer list.

name: Konstantin Petrovich Ivanov-Trinadtsaty
role: Rurik’s last commander in battle and Peresvet’s captain on her final voyage in 1916
bio:
Lieutenant Konstantin Ivanov did not begin Rurik’s last voyage as her appointed captain. He was a gunnery officer who took command during the battle of 1 (14) August 1904, after Captain Yevgeny Trusov was killed and the senior officers were successively incapacitated. The Vladivostok cruiser lost steering control and came under concentrated Japanese fire.

The wounded Ivanov directed her resistance and, when it could no longer continue, ordered the ship scuttled. Japanese sailors rescued him; captivity and prolonged medical treatment followed. The number in his name had originally been the navy’s ordinary way of distinguishing officers with the same surname. “Trinadtsaty”, meaning “Thirteenth”, was later made part of his family name and that of his descendants. He continued serving after the war, including in submarines. In 1916 he commanded Peresvet, bought back from Japan, on her last voyage, surviving her loss to mines off Port Said. He spent his final years in France and died in Lyon.

name: Andrei Petrovich Shter
role: Novik officer and memoirist of her final voyage
bio:
Lieutenant Andrei Shter left one of the most detailed accounts of service aboard Novik. He was a watch officer and commanded the after group of guns. In 1904 he fought off Port Arthur, took part in the July breakout and made the final voyage to Sakhalin.

After the battle off Korsakov, Novik had to be scuttled. The war did not end there for the survivors: they faced an arduous journey across Sakhalin and a return to Vladivostok. Shter described these events in On the Cruiser Novik. It is a participant’s account, with his own viewpoint and judgements of his superiors, rather than an impartial history of the entire squadron. Shter later commanded submarines and torpedo boats. In 1907 he was killed aboard the torpedo boat Skory during the Vladivostok uprising. His book outlived him and preserved his crew’s experience.

name: Nikolai Kuzmich Chernyshev
role: Commander of Sevastopol at the start of the Russo-Japanese War
bio:
Nikolai Chernyshev commanded the battleship Sevastopol when war with Japan began in January 1904. He had taken command the previous autumn. The ship’s first sorties and battles therefore fell under his command, although her final months of resistance and scuttling are usually associated with Nikolai Essen.

The change of captain came in the spring, after Stepan Makarov’s arrival. Chernyshev was removed from the ship in March; his service chronology records his release on grounds of illness. Essen transferred from Novik to Sevastopol. These two periods must be distinguished: the battleship’s actions in White Wolf Bay at the end of the siege did not take place under Chernyshev. He died in St Petersburg in 1905. Some reference works mistakenly give his patronymic as “Kirillovich”; Sevastopol’s captain was Nikolai Kuzmich.

name: A. A. Brovtsyn
role: Pallada’s watch officer on the first night of the war
bio:
Lieutenant Brovtsyn was Pallada’s watch officer on the night of 26–27 January 1904, Old Style. He spotted the approaching Japanese torpedo boats. The cruiser sounded the alarm, but the attackers’ navigation lights made identification difficult: fire was opened when a torpedo’s track became visible. A hit caused fire and flooding aboard Pallada.

Brovtsyn later commanded the torpedo boat Grozovoy. After the July battle she escaped to Shanghai, where the neutral Chinese authorities disarmed her. The officer’s war had begun on a badly damaged cruiser and ended on a small vessel outside blockaded Port Arthur. He subsequently continued serving in the Baltic and Black Seas. Available biographies disagree on the expansion of his patronymic; the initials used in the study of Pallada are retained here.

name: Vasily Arsenyevich Boisman
role: Commander of Peresvet, who died of his wounds in Japanese captivity
bio:
By the start of the war, Vasily Boisman had served for many years in the Far East, conducting hydrographic work, commanding torpedo vessels and working in the Port Arthur naval port. In 1902 he received command of Peresvet. His service at the fortress began long before the siege and cannot be reduced to a single battle.

In the battle of 28 July, Old Style, Peresvet carried the flag of junior flag officer Pavel Ukhtomsky. Boisman was seriously wounded, and executive officer Apollon Dmitriyev took over the ship. Her captain was treated in Port Arthur before sharing the garrison’s fate as a Japanese prisoner. He died in Matsuyama in 1905. His grave in the Russian cemetery survives as a place of remembrance. His story exposes a particular divide between a battleship’s fate and her captain’s: the ship was raised by the Japanese and served again; Boisman never returned home.

name: Apollon Apollonovich Dmitriyev
role: Peresvet’s executive officer, who replaced her wounded captain
bio:
Apollon Dmitriyev began the defence of Port Arthur as commander of the torpedo boat Leytenant Burakov. In spring 1904 he became Peresvet’s executive officer. This was the captain’s closest assistant, responsible for the ship’s internal organisation and ready to replace him in battle.

That replacement became necessary after the battle of 28 July, Old Style. Vasily Boisman was seriously wounded, and Dmitriyev temporarily assumed command of the battleship. He too suffered concussion and received hospital treatment. After the fortress fell he became a Japanese prisoner. On returning, he served in the Black Sea, commanding the destroyer Leytenant Shestakov and later the battleship Ioann Zlatoust. He died in Moscow in September 1914. In Peresvet’s history, his name marks the continuation of service aboard after her wounded captain could no longer remain on the bridge.

name: Mikhail Borisovich Cherkassky
role: Diana midshipman and later chief of staff of the Baltic Fleet
bio:
Prince Mikhail Cherkassky served aboard Diana before she reached the Far East. A Naval Corps graduate of 1901, he was a watch officer and acting junior torpedo officer. At Port Arthur the young midshipman found himself amid events whose decisions lay with much more senior commanders.

After the battle of 28 July, Old Style, Diana sailed south. Cherkassky took part in discussions about proceeding towards French ports, and the cruiser eventually reached Saigon. He later received gunnery and higher naval education and served on the Baltic Fleet staff during the First World War. In 1917 he became its chief of staff and a rear admiral. After leaving the navy he went to Ukraine, where he died during the Civil War. The Port Arthur midshipman had risen to head the staff of a major naval force.

name: Vasily Nilovich Cherkasov
role: Peresvet’s gunnery officer and memoirist of the siege
bio:
Vasily Cherkasov began the war as Sevastopol’s senior gunnery officer and transferred to the same post aboard Peresvet in spring 1904. His work connected the bridge with the gun crews: the organisation of the gunnery service affected how the ship could fight.

Cherkasov left notes on the defence of Port Arthur. He wrote about firing, damage, decisions by commanders and everyday service often overlooked in broad accounts of battles. After siege artillery destroyed Peresvet, he supervised shell production on the Tiger Peninsula. His memoirs show how a naval gunner continued working for the defence after losing his battleship. He later served in both the imperial and Soviet navies. He should not be confused with his younger brother Pyotr Nilovich, captain of the gunboat Sivuch during the First World War.

name: Alexei Mikhailovich Nirod
role: Varyag’s midshipman and rangefinder officer, killed at Chemulpo
bio:
Count Alexei Nirod was the cruiser Varyag’s junior navigating officer. A Naval Corps graduate of 1902, he was only beginning his career when war broke out. During the Battle of Chemulpo on 27 January (9 February) 1904, he was assigned to measure the distance to the Japanese ships.

A rangefinder officer worked in an exposed position: the gunners needed his measurements to set their sights. Nirod was on the forward bridge and was killed by a Japanese shell early in the battle. His name survives in casualty lists and on photographs from before the revolution. An archival photographic record identifies him as Alexei Mikhailovich; the patronymic “Alexeyevich” found in some retellings is mistaken. His short biography recalls that Varyag’s battle involved not only the captain’s decision but the work of young specialists under fire.

name: Ivan Petrovich Uspensky
role: Commander of Poltava during the defence of Port Arthur
bio:
Ivan Uspensky commanded Poltava during the Russo-Japanese War. A graduate of the Naval School and Mine Officer Class, he had previously sailed in various seas and commanded the torpedo cruiser Vsadnik and gunboat Mandzhur. His service aboard Poltava joined the history of one of the older battleships on which the Port Arthur Squadron depended.

The ship fought at sea and returned to the fortress after the failed July breakout. Like the other vessels, she then had to operate within a land siege. Japanese heavy artillery put Poltava out of action in late 1904. Uspensky survived captivity in Japan and, after returning, held posts in the naval shipbuilding and supply administration. He later commanded the naval forces in the Pacific, became a vice admiral in 1910 and retired the following year.

name: Sergei Ivanovich Lutonin
role: Poltava’s executive officer and memoirist of the Port Arthur Squadron
bio:
Sergei Lutonin was Poltava’s executive officer in 1903–1904. Previously he had graduated from the Naval School and Gunnery Officer Class, sailed aboard Vityaz and served on Sevastopol and the gunboat Gilyak. He entered the war as an experienced ship’s officer and was promoted to captain second rank at the beginning of 1904.

Lutonin’s memoirs describe service in the Port Arthur Squadron and the Battle of the Yellow Sea in detail. His viewpoint from one of the ships makes his testimony particularly useful alongside captains’ reports and staff documents. His personal judgements should be distinguished from the established sequence of events. After the war he commanded the gunboat Zaporozhets, later returned to service during the First World War and headed the Kola base. Poltava’s history survives in his account as well as in drawings and damage reports.

name: Alexander Rostislavovich Rodionov
role: Bayan’s first commander during her construction in France
bio:
Alexander Rodionov commanded Bayan before the cruiser reached Port Arthur and entered the war. His appointment covered her construction in France in 1899–1902. It meant working with a ship that was not yet complete: preparing the crew, supervising execution of the design and taking part in acceptance of the future warship.

Before Bayan, Rodionov had commanded Rurik and Pallada and served on naval staffs. In 1902 he moved to the Main Administration of Shipbuilding and Supplies and became a rear admiral. Robert Viren took over the cruiser, bringing her to the Far East and fighting in her in 1904. Rodionov should therefore not be counted among Bayan’s wartime crew at Port Arthur: his contribution belonged to the ship’s creation. His patronymic was Rostislavovich, as recorded in the appendix to the cruiser’s monograph.

name: Vladimir Ivanovich Litvinov
role: Commander of the training detachment that helped Messina in 1908
bio:
Admiral Vladimir Litvinov’s connection with Tsesarevich belongs to the period after the Russo-Japanese War. In 1908 the battleship formed part of the training detachment he led in the Mediterranean. Naval cadets, future officers, were gaining practical experience aboard the ships. When an earthquake destroyed Messina on 28 December, New Style, the training voyage became a rescue operation.

Litvinov directed the detachment to the stricken city. Sailors cleared rubble, carried out the wounded and transported people to safety; naval doctors worked ashore and aboard. Port Arthur’s former flagship was needed as a transport, hospital and rescuers’ base rather than as an artillery platform. Litvinov had served in the navy since the 1870s and commanded various ships, reaching the rank of admiral in 1916. Assistance to Messina remains the best-known episode of his career.

name: Oskar Viktorovich Stark
role: Commander of the Pacific Squadron at the opening of the 1904 war
bio:
The Russian squadron faced the first Japanese torpedo attack at Port Arthur under Oskar Stark’s command. On the night of 26–27 January (8–9 February) 1904, Retvizan, Tsesarevich and Pallada were damaged; Stark flew his flag aboard Petropavlovsk.

Born at Helsinki in 1846, he graduated from the Naval Cadet Corps and served for many years in the Far East. Before taking command of the squadron, he headed Port Arthur Port and therefore knew the base long before the war. Yet knowing the harbour could not resolve the difficult question of preparing for an attack while the political leadership still hoped to avoid one.

After the opening battles, Stepan Makarov replaced him. Stark continued serving in Russia and retired as an admiral in 1908. After the revolution he lived in Finland, dying at Helsinki in 1928. Popular accounts often remember only the commander whose fleet was caught at anchor when war began. Behind that appointment, however, lay decades of service and work on the very base the squadron would have to defend.

name: Kirill Vladimirovich Romanov
role: Grand duke and Makarov’s staff officer, rescued from Petropavlovsk
bio:
Grand Duke Kirill Vladimirovich was among those rescued when Petropavlovsk sank off Port Arthur on 31 March (13 April) 1904. A cousin of Nicholas II, he served on Makarov’s staff and was aboard the flagship when she struck a mine.

Born at Tsarskoye Selo in 1876, he received a naval education and made his military career at sea. He reached Port Arthur after the war had begun and served there for only a few weeks before the disaster. His later memoir of the sinking is a survivor’s testimony, rather than a complete account of everything that happened aboard.

During the First World War he commanded the Guards Naval Crew. After the revolution he left Russia and became a central figure in the émigré disputes over the dynasty. In 1924 he proclaimed himself emperor in exile, a claim that was not universally accepted. He died at Paris in 1938. His political biography often overshadows Port Arthur: behind the later claimant to the throne stood a naval officer who had survived the death of his commander and most of the people aboard his flagship.

name: Amable Lagane
role: French naval architect who designed Tsesarevich
bio:
Tsesarevich acquired her French appearance long before reaching Port Arthur. Her designer was Amable Lagane, an engineer at the La Seyne shipyard near Toulon. High sides, heavy masts and turret mounting for every secondary gun distinguished her from the Poltava-class battleships.

Antoine Jean Amable Lagane was born at Gourdon in southern France in 1838. He entered the École Polytechnique in 1856 and then chose naval architecture. In 1865 he joined the Forges et Chantiers de la Méditerranée, becoming chief engineer of its La Seyne yards in 1872. They built warships and merchant vessels for different countries; the Russian order of the late 1890s belonged to this international business.

Tsesarevich was built in France under Russian specialists’ supervision. After reaching the Far East, she fought in the 1904 war and became Vitgeft’s flagship. Lagane died at Toulon in 1910. His connection with Port Arthur was through design and the shipyard: he neither commanded the battleship nor belonged to her crew.

name: Nikolai Alexandrovich Matusevich
role: Vitgeft’s chief of staff, wounded aboard Tsesarevich
bio:
At the Battle of the Yellow Sea on 28 July (10 August) 1904, squadron chief of staff Nikolai Matusevich was wounded aboard Tsesarevich. Vitgeft was killed, the flagship lost control of the formation, and after the battle the ship reached German-held Tsingtao, where she was disarmed.

Born at Nikolayev in 1852, Matusevich began his service in the Black Sea. His career included the Russo-Turkish War, ship commands and work with mine and torpedo weapons. Before the war with Japan he commanded Rurik, then headed a torpedo-boat detachment at Port Arthur. In spring 1904 he became a rear admiral and the squadron’s chief of staff. That office supported orders, communications and the work of the formation; it did not make him captain of Tsesarevich, which Nikolai Ivanov commanded.

After the war he continued serving, headed the Pacific naval forces in 1908–1909 and then joined the Admiralty Council. He died at Sevastopol in 1912. Port Arthur brought severe wounds and the loss of his flagship, but did not end his naval career.

name: Ewald Antonovich Stackelberg
role: Commander of Diana’s voyage to the Far East and later of the Vladivostok cruiser detachment
bio:
Diana reached the Far East in 1903 with Rear Admiral Ewald Stackelberg’s detachment. For the new cruiser, the voyage led towards war; for the admiral it was another period of Far Eastern service.

Born in 1847 into a Baltic German noble family, Stackelberg graduated from the Naval School and circumnavigated the world aboard the corvette Bayan. This was a steam-and-sail corvette, not the armoured cruiser that later fought under the same name at Port Arthur. During the Russo-Turkish War he took part in mine operations on the Danube, subsequently commanded ships and served in the Pacific.

In 1903 he headed the Vladivostok cruiser detachment. Illness forced him to relinquish command at the beginning of the war in 1904; Karl Jessen later commanded the formation. Back in the Baltic, Stackelberg sat on commissions examining naval operations and the war’s results. He retired as a vice admiral in 1908 and died in 1909. In Diana’s history his name belongs chiefly to the voyage to her station, rather than command of the cruiser in the Port Arthur battles.

name: Alexei Nikolayevich Krylov
role: Naval scientist who helped assess Askold’s condition after the war
bio:
In Askold’s final chapters, Alexei Krylov’s name is associated with a choice: restore the old cruiser or scrap her. In the early 1920s a commission including him inspected the ship to decide whether rebuilding was justified. Repairs were judged too expensive, and Askold was sold for scrap in 1922.

Born at Visyaga in Simbirsk province in 1863, Krylov graduated from the Naval School and then the Naval Academy. He specialized in calculations governing a ship’s behaviour in waves, stability and safety. From 1900 he headed the Experimental Tank, where future ships’ properties were tested using models; later he chaired the Naval Technical Committee. He became an academician in 1916.

After the revolution he continued research and teaching, also working in applied mathematics. He died in 1945. For Askold, his assessment concerned the final choice between repair and demolition; for the scientist, it was one of many tasks requiring maritime experience to be combined with calculations of cost and technical condition.

name: Tōgō Heihachirō
role: Commander-in-chief of Japan’s Combined Fleet in the war of 1904–1905
bio:
Tōgō was born in Kagoshima, into a samurai family of the Satsuma domain. He fought in the Boshin War and went to Britain in 1871 to study naval affairs. During the Sino-Japanese War he commanded the cruiser Naniwa. His appointment to command the Combined Fleet in 1903 followed many years of shipboard and staff service.

During the Russo-Japanese War, Tōgō directed operations against the squadron at Port Arthur. He flew his flag in Mikasa, whose captain was Hikojirō Ijichi. The blockade, the Battle of the Yellow Sea and the interception of Russian reinforcements were separate stages of the campaign. On 27–28 May 1905 his fleet defeated the Russian forces at Tsushima.

Tōgō became an admiral of the fleet in 1913. He later headed the institution responsible for the crown prince’s education and retained influence in the Japanese navy. He died in 1934. In Port Arthur’s history his role was chiefly that of the fortress’s naval opponent; other officers directed the siege on land.

name: Akiyama Saneyuki
role: Combined Fleet staff officer who helped prepare naval operations
bio:
Akiyama was born in Matsuyama, into a former samurai family. His elder brother Yoshifuru entered the army; Saneyuki became a naval officer. After graduating from the Naval Academy, he served in the Sino-Japanese War. In 1897 he went to the United States to study naval theory and American naval practice, and observed operations during the Spanish-American War.

On returning to Japan, he taught strategy and tactics at the Naval War College. During the war of 1904–1905 he served on Tōgō’s Combined Fleet staff. His work aboard Mikasa concerned operational planning and staff duties. He helped develop the fleet’s operations that culminated in Tsushima, while Ijichi commanded the ship and Tōgō made the commander-in-chief’s decisions.

Akiyama continued his naval career after the war. He headed the Bureau of Naval Affairs in 1914 and became a vice-admiral in 1917. He died in February 1918. His career reveals work that photographs of turrets and bridges cannot show: gathering information, preparing plans and turning a commander’s decisions into staff action.
