name: Hikojirō Ijichi
role: Captain of Mikasa during the Russo-Japanese War
bio:
Ijichi came from Satsuma and studied at the Japanese Naval Academy. His service included shipboard assignments, overseas postings and teaching at the Naval War College. He participated in the Sino-Japanese War.

During the war against Russia he commanded Mikasa. Tōgō and the Combined Fleet staff were aboard the same battleship, making it easy to confuse three different responsibilities. Tōgō commanded the fleet, the staff prepared and communicated his decisions, and Ijichi was responsible for the ship itself. The Mikasa museum names him among the bridge officers depicted before the Battle of Tsushima.

Ijichi continued serving after the war, commanding the training squadron on overseas cruises in 1909–1910. Reports issued in his name from Seattle and Australia survive in the Japanese archives. He reached the rank of vice-admiral and died in January 1912. His biography restores to the flagship its own captain, often overshadowed by Tōgō.

name: Nashiba Tokioki
role: Rear-admiral whose flag was in Hatsuse when she sank
bio:
Nashiba came from the Chōshū domain. Before entering the navy, he fought in the Boshin War and worked in civilian agencies concerned with surveying. He joined the navy in 1880. During the Sino-Japanese War he served in Chiyoda, and later commanded several ships, including Hatsuse.

By the 1904 campaign he was a rear-admiral commanding a formation. On 15 May Japanese battleships struck a Russian minefield off Port Arthur. Hatsuse and Yashima were lost. Nashiba was aboard Hatsuse and survived. A paired portrait in a wartime publication explicitly distinguishes Admiral Nashiba from Captain Nakao: an admiral flying his flag aboard a ship was not necessarily its captain.

After the war Nashiba became a vice-admiral and a baron, and served in the House of Peers. He died in 1928. The 1924 death date found in some English references conflicts with the Japanese library attribution of his writings, which gives 1850–1928.

name: Sakamoto Hajime
role: Captain of Yashima when she sank; participant in salvage work at Port Arthur
bio:
Sakamoto was born in Tosa, now Kōchi Prefecture. He attended the Naval Academy, served in the Sino-Japanese War, held an appointment in Fuji and was executive officer of Yashima. In October 1903 he returned to Yashima as her captain.

On 15 May 1904 Yashima struck mines off Port Arthur. Efforts to save her failed, and she sank. Sakamoto survived and later received an appointment in the defence of Dalian Bay. The July 1905 issue of the American naval journal Proceedings singled him out among the specialists raising Russian ships, particularly Bayan. It identified him as Yashima’s former captain, linking the two episodes of his service.

After the war Sakamoto headed naval arsenals, became a vice-admiral and commanded the Port Arthur naval station. He died in 1948. His connection with the city continued after the loss of his ship, through salvage work and the organisation of the Japanese naval base.

name: Nakao Yū
role: Captain of Hatsuse when she sank on 15 May 1904
bio:
Nakao came from the Hiroshima area. He entered the Naval Academy in 1871, served aboard training and warships, and later held staff appointments. Before the war against Russia he commanded Takachiho, Chitose and Asama. He took command of Hatsuse in autumn 1903.

On 15 May 1904 the battleship struck a Russian minefield off Port Arthur and sank. Nakao survived, as did Rear-Admiral Nashiba, who was also aboard. Their paired portrait appeared in an English history of the war; a copy is held by the International Research Center for Japanese Studies. Its caption names Nakao as captain and Nashiba as admiral, a useful distinction when reading accounts of the flagship’s loss.

Nakao continued in shore and staff posts. A 1908 archival file identifies him as a rear-admiral in the Sasebo port administration; he later became a vice-admiral. He died in 1926. His full name is Nakao Yū, 中尾雄. English captions from the war often gave only his surname.

name: Gustave Canet
role: French engineer whose artillery systems were manufactured for the Russian navy
bio:
Canet was born in Belfort, trained as an engineer at the École Centrale in Paris and began his career on the railways. After the Franco-Prussian War he turned to artillery. He studied arms manufacture in Britain, then headed the ordnance department of Forges et Chantiers de la Méditerranée. He later worked for Schneider.

For the Russian navy, his surname became the name of a family of quick-firing guns. In 1891 the Naval Ministry acquired manufacturing rights for his 120 mm and 152 mm systems; production followed at the Obukhov Works. In the Port Arthur squadron, these guns formed the main armament of several cruisers and the secondary armament of battleships. They also served ashore.

Canet designed more than barrels: a quick-firing gun depended on its breech, mounting and recoil mechanism. His name on a Russian gun identifies the system’s origin, rather than necessarily its place of manufacture. He died in 1908; the weapons remained in service much longer. A French engineer, a Russian factory and different shipboard mountings belong to the same production history.

name: Anton Frantsevich Brink
role: Naval gun designer and chief inspector of naval artillery
bio:
Brink graduated from the Mikhailovsky Artillery Academy in 1878. He then worked at the Obukhov Works, studying both gun design and the practical possibilities of manufacture. In 1886 he moved to the artillery department of the Naval Technical Committee. The combination of theoretical training and factory experience shaped his subsequent work.

In the early 1890s Brink designed a 12-inch naval gun 40 calibres long. Makarov commissioned his calculations; discussions with the Obukhov Works produced the design tested in 1895. These guns became the main armament of many Russian battleships, including vessels of the Port Arthur squadron. Brink also helped develop eight-inch guns. His work should not be reduced to one model or confused with that of its manufacturer.

He later headed naval artillery, taught and wrote on gun strength and internal ballistics. He died in 1925. His name was Anton Frantsevich: the initials A. F. in the relevant artillery literature refer to him. Alexei Fyodorovich Brink, known for his work on shell fuzes, was a different man.

name: Benjamin Berkeley Hotchkiss
role: American ordnance engineer who established manufacturing in France
bio:
Hotchkiss was born in Connecticut and began his career in the American arms industry, developing artillery ammunition. In 1867 he moved to France and established the enterprise later known as Hotchkiss et Cie. His work included a revolving cannon with several barrels, intended in part for naval use.

Russian documents rendered his surname as Gochkis. By the beginning of the 1904 war, single-barrel 47 mm guns of this family had long been imported and manufactured in Russia. The Central Naval Museum holds a naval gun made at the Obukhov Works in 1892. Small quick-firing guns aboard the Port Arthur squadron’s ships were intended chiefly for defence against torpedo boats.

The engineer died in Paris in 1885, so the system’s name does not imply his personal involvement in later modifications. Production continued after his death. The single-barrel 47 mm gun, the earlier revolving cannon and the later Hotchkiss machine gun must be distinguished: the same company name covers different designs and different periods of the firm’s work.

name: William George Armstrong
role: British engineer and industrialist who founded the Elswick armaments business
bio:
Armstrong was born in Newcastle and first worked as a solicitor. His interest in hydraulic machinery drew him into engineering. His works on the Tyne manufactured industrial equipment, artillery and warships. In 1859 he was knighted after giving his gun patents to the government.

Armstrong’s businesses became international arms suppliers. Their connections with Japan were particularly close, as the country bought ships and artillery for its new navy. Fred Jane’s 1904 book describes the Elswick 12-inch guns of Japanese battleships, including Mikasa. This industrial origin of the opposing fleet’s armament is the connection between Armstrong’s name and Port Arthur.

Armstrong died in 1900, before the Russo-Japanese War. It would be wrong to call him the personal designer of every later weapon made by the firm: other engineers continued its work. His house at Cragside preserves another side of his activities, including hydraulics and early electricity. The international arms business and its founder’s life belong together, but their timelines differ.

name: Katō Tomosaburō
role: Combined Fleet chief of staff at Tsushima; later prime minister of Japan
bio:
Katō was born in Hiroshima, into a samurai family. He entered the Naval Academy in 1873. During the Sino-Japanese War he served as chief gunnery officer of the cruiser Yoshino. His subsequent career joined shipboard artillery, staff duties and national politics.

During the Russo-Japanese War, Katō became chief of staff of Tōgō’s Combined Fleet. The Mikasa museum names him among the officers depicted on the bridge before Tsushima. He assisted the commander-in-chief in directing the fleet; Ijichi remained captain of the battleship. Katō’s responsibility concerned the formation, rather than command of the individual ship.

After the war he was navy minister in several cabinets. He led Japan’s delegation to the Washington Conference in 1921 and became prime minister in 1922, retaining the naval portfolio. His government accepted the Washington Naval Treaty and decided to withdraw troops from Siberia. He died in August 1923. His career carries the history of the war into an era when states sought to limit fleet sizes by agreement.

name: Uryū Sotokichi
role: Commander of the Japanese squadron that fought Varyag at Chemulpo
bio:
Uryū received his naval education in the United States, graduating from the Naval Academy at Annapolis in 1881. He returned to serve in the Japanese navy and commanded ships. His name appears in different European spellings, including Uriu and Uryū; in Japanese it is 瓜生外吉.

At the beginning of the Russo-Japanese War, Rear-Admiral Uryū commanded the squadron off the Korean port of Chemulpo, now Incheon. Japanese ships covered troop landings and controlled the exit from the anchorage where Varyag and Koreets were stationed. Uryū demanded that the Russian ships leave and warned that he would attack if they stayed. The battle took place on 9 February 1904 New Style; the Russian ships returned to the anchorage and were abandoned by their crews.

Uryū continued his career after the war and reached the rank of admiral. He died in November 1937. His connection with the Port Arthur squadron belongs to a separate episode in Korea: Chemulpo was not Port Arthur’s roadstead, and Varyag was away from the Russian fleet’s main base on the day of the battle.

name: Pavel Mikhailovich Dmitriev
role: Chief engineer of the destroyer Strashny
bio:
By the spring of 1904 Pavel Dmitriev, a graduate of Moscow Technical School, was back in naval service. Recalled from the reserve to Port Arthur, he became chief engineer of Strashny, responsible for keeping its machinery running.

On the night of 12–13 April 1904 (30–31 March Old Style), the destroyer fell behind its detachment. At dawn it fought Japanese warships and sank. Dmitriev died alongside the other officers. In 1905 a new ship was launched under his name, Inzhener-Mekhanik Dmitriev.

role: Captain of the destroyer Strashny in its final engagement
bio:
Captain 2nd Rank Konstantin Yurasovsky took command of Strashny at Port Arthur in 1904. The destroyer had only just entered service and was already scouting off the Kwantung Peninsula.

On the night of 12–13 April 1904 (30–31 March Old Style), Strashny lost contact with the Russian ships and met a Japanese detachment at dawn. Yurasovsky was killed and Lieutenant Maleyev took command. New destroyers later took the names of both officers and their chief engineer, Pavel Dmitriev.

name: Sergei Alexandrovich Rashevsky
role: Military engineer and diarist of the Port Arthur siege
bio:
In the spring of 1904 Lieutenant Colonel Sergei Rashevsky served as an engineer at Port Arthur. From Golden Hill he saw Petropavlovsk sink in the outer roadstead. In his entry for 13 April (31 March Old Style), he recalled how observers ashore initially took the smoke above the battleship for gunfire.

During the siege Rashevsky worked on the defences with Roman Kondratenko. On 15 December (2 December Old Style) they were killed at Fort No. II when a Japanese shell burst inside a casemate. Rashevsky's diary was found after his death and first published in 1954.

name: Sergei Alexandrovich Korsakov
role: Fortress artillery officer who photographed Port Arthur
bio:
In 1904 Sergei Korsakov served with the Kwantung fortress artillery and photographed the defence of Port Arthur. His name survives in archival captions for photographs taken at the fortress.

In 1914 the magazine Iskry published a photograph of the loss of Petropavlovsk and credited Korsakov as its photographer. In his account of the same morning, the officer Mikhail Lilie names another photographer, the military engineer Sergei Rashevsky.

name: Vasily Ivanovich Nemirovich-Danchenko
role: Russkoye Slovo's war correspondent at Port Arthur
bio:
In the spring of 1904 Vasily Nemirovich-Danchenko arrived in Port Arthur on assignment for Russkoye Slovo. He had already covered the Russo-Turkish War. From the Far East he sent dispatches on the fighting and on life inside the fortress.

His account of the journey, To the War: From St Petersburg to Port Arthur, appeared that same year. He was still reporting during the First World War. He spent his last years in Prague, where he died in 1936.

name: Zinovy Petrovich Rozhestvensky
role: Commander of the Second Pacific Squadron on its voyage and at Tsushima
bio:
In 1904 Zinovy Rozhestvensky led the Second Pacific Squadron from the Baltic to reinforce the Russian fleet in the Far East. Port Arthur fell while the ships were making their way around Africa and across the Indian Ocean. The squadron's new destination was Vladivostok.

At Tsushima on 27 May 1905 (14 May Old Style), Rozhestvensky was aboard his flagship Knyaz Suvorov. The destroyer Buiny took the badly wounded admiral aboard. He was transferred to Bedovy and taken prisoner by the Japanese. In 1906 he was acquitted at the trial over Bedovy's surrender.

name: Nikolai Ivanovich Nebogatov
role: Commander of the Third Pacific Squadron who surrendered four ships after Tsushima
bio:
In 1905 Rear Admiral Nikolai Nebogatov led the Third Pacific Squadron out of the Baltic. Off the coast of Vietnam it joined Rozhestvensky's Second Squadron, with Nebogatov commanding his battleship detachment under his flag on Imperator Nikolai I.

On the morning of 28 May (15 May Old Style), the second day of the Battle of Tsushima, the Japanese fleet surrounded the ships still with Nebogatov. The admiral gave the order to surrender. In 1906 a court sentenced him to death. The sentence was commuted to ten years in prison and Nebogatov was pardoned in 1909.

name: Vasily Vasilyevich Ignatius
role: Captain of Knyaz Suvorov and marine artist
bio:
Years before Tsushima, Lieutenant Vasily Ignatius drew the ships he served on. His drawings appeared in St Petersburg in the album The Russian Fleet. He later served in the Pacific as executive officer of the cruiser Razboynik.

In 1904 Ignatius took Knyaz Suvorov from the Baltic to the Far East. The squadron commander, Zinovy Rozhestvensky, flew his flag on the ship. Ignatius captained the battleship and died at Tsushima on 27 May 1905 (14 May Old Style).

name: Nikolai Mikhailovich Bukhvostov
role: Captain of Imperator Aleksandr III
bio:
In the autumn of 1904 Captain 1st Rank Nikolai Bukhvostov sailed from the Baltic aboard Imperator Aleksandr III. The battleship drew its sailors from the Naval Guards Crew, where Bukhvostov had served before his appointment.

In the Tsushima Strait on 27 May 1905 (14 May Old Style), Aleksandr III took the lead of the Russian column after the damaged flagship fell out of line. The battleship went down that evening. Bukhvostov and his entire crew died.

name: Pyotr Osipovich Serebrennikov
role: Captain of Borodino
bio:
Pyotr Serebrennikov took command of Borodino while it was still under construction, before the Russo-Japanese War. In 1904, by then a captain 1st rank, he sailed from the Baltic in the First Battleship Division of the Second Pacific Squadron.

On 27 May 1905 (14 May Old Style), Borodino briefly led the Russian column at Tsushima. The ship sank that evening. Serebrennikov died. Semyon Yushchin, a petty officer, was the battleship's only survivor.

name: Nikolai Viktorovich Yung
role: Captain of Oryol
bio:
In 1904 Captain 1st Rank Nikolai Yung sailed for the Far East in command of the new battleship Oryol. Three other Borodino-class ships sailed in the same division of the Second Pacific Squadron.

Yung was mortally wounded on the first day of the Battle of Tsushima. The next morning the damaged Oryol was among the ships Rear Admiral Nikolai Nebogatov surrendered to the Japanese fleet. Yung died of his wounds.

name: Semyon Semyonovich Yushchin
role: Petty officer in charge of a mast top and survivor of the battleship Borodino
bio:
On the evening of 27 May 1905 (14 May Old Style) the battleship Borodino capsized and sank in the Tsushima Strait. Semyon Yushchin escaped through an opening in the side. He later told the Main Naval Staff that the crew of a Japanese destroyer pulled him from the water. Records of the loss name him as the only survivor.

In Japanese captivity Yushchin met Aleksei Novikov, who later wrote as Novikov-Priboy. Novikov based his account of Borodino's sinking, published in 1906, on Yushchin's testimony. The Mordovian regional museum holds his documents and awards. Yushchin returned to his native Alkaevo and died in 1935.

name: Dmitri Ivanovich Mendeleev
role: Chemist and author of Cherished Thoughts
bio:
Dmitri Mendeleev was born in Tobolsk in 1834. He taught chemistry at St Petersburg University and formulated the periodic law in 1869. In the 1890s he became head of the Central Bureau of Weights and Measures, where he helped develop Russia’s system of measurement standards.

When the Russo-Japanese War broke out, Mendeleev devoted a chapter of Cherished Thoughts to it. He wrote about the importance of access to the Pacific and the need for industrial development in Russia. He died in St Petersburg in 1907.

name: Boris Vasilyevich Ananich
role: Historian of the Russian economy and author of Banking Houses in Russia
bio:
Boris Ananich was born in Leningrad in 1931 and graduated from the history faculty of Leningrad University. In 1956 he joined the Leningrad branch of the Soviet Academy of Sciences’ Institute of History, now the St Petersburg Institute of History of the Russian Academy of Sciences. The Academy elected him a full member in 1994.

Ananich studied public finances and private enterprise in the Russian Empire. In Banking Houses in Russia, 1860–1914, he traced the history of family-run banking firms. He died in St Petersburg in 2015.
